method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
steps: Identify the useful output and the total input (both energy, or both power, never mixed).
Divide: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Multiply by 100 if the question wants a percentage.
Sense check: efficiency is always below 1 (100%).
method_card.content:
Efficiency tells you how much of the energy put into a device comes out in the useful form you want.

efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Use energy values or power values, but never mix them. The answer is a decimal; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

It can never be more than 1 (100%): if yours is, you divided the wrong way round. Wasted energy = total input − useful output, and it ends up warming the surroundings.

exam_context.frequency: Very common: efficiency appears in almost every Paper 1

gold.display: A crane motor with an efficiency of 0.75 lifts a 120 kg steel beam to a height of 20 m. Calculate the total electrical energy input to the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Useful output = GPE = mgh = 120 × 9.8 × 20 = 23,520 J. Total input = useful ÷ efficiency = 23,520 ÷ 0.75 = 31,360 J.
Don't multiply useful by efficiency. Total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

gold.hint: Find the GPE first (mgh), then divide it by the efficiency.

guided_steps.say: Two equations chained. First the useful output, the GPE gained: \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply by the height to get the GPE.

guided_steps.say: That GPE is the useful output. Rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.done: Back to 23,520 J, so the input is right.

guided_steps.say: So the total electrical energy input is 31,360 J.

gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 25 m/s. The engine has an efficiency of 0.30. Calculate the total chemical energy released from the fuel.

misconceptions.message: First find KE gained: ½ × 1200 × 25² = ½ × 1200 × 625 = 375,000 J. This is the useful output. Total input = 375,000 ÷ 0.30 = 1,250,000 J.
Remember to square the speed: 25² = 625, not 25 × 2 = 50.

gold.hint: Square the speed for KE, then divide the KE by the efficiency.

guided_steps.say: First the useful output, the kinetic energy gained: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed first.

guided_steps.hint: Half of mass times speed squared.

guided_steps.say: That KE is the useful output. Rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.done: Back to 375,000 J, so the input is right.

guided_steps.say: So the total chemical energy released is 1,250,000 J (1.25 MJ).

gold.display: A solar panel converts sunlight into 240 W of useful electrical power. The panel is 20% efficient. The Sun delivers 800 W/m² to the panel. Calculate the area of the panel.

misconceptions.message: Total input power = useful ÷ efficiency = 240 ÷ 0.20 = 1200 W. Area = total power ÷ power per m² = 1200 ÷ 800 = 1.5 m².
First find total power input, then divide by the solar intensity to find the area.

gold.hint: Find the total power (useful ÷ efficiency), then divide by 800 for the area.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First the total power the panel must receive: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.
The Sun delivers 800 W for every m². Area = total power ÷ power per m².

guided_steps.hint: Should return the total power needed.
guided_steps.done: 1.5 m² collects 1200 W, so the area is right.

guided_steps.say: So the panel area is 1.5 m².

gold.display: A pump with a power rating of 600 W and an efficiency of 0.70 lifts water to a height of 8 m for 5 minutes. Calculate the mass of water lifted. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Remember to account for the efficiency, only 70% of the input energy lifts the water.

gold.hint: Convert minutes to seconds, find useful energy, then use mgh rearranged.

guided_steps.say: Several steps. First convert the time, because power is joules per second.
Total energy supplied = power × time.
Now the finish. Only 70% of that energy lifts the water. Useful energy = efficiency × total.
This useful energy is the GPE, \(E_p = mgh\), so \(m = \frac{E_p}{gh}\). First find \(gh\).

guided_steps.hint: Useful energy over gh; round to 1 decimal place.
guided_steps.done: So the mass is about 1607.1 kg.

guided_steps.say: Check: 1607 kg of water lifted 8 m gains close to 126,000 J of GPE, matching the useful energy, so the answer is right (given to 1 d.p.).

gold.display: Kettle A is 88% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 2000 W. Kettle B is 95% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 1800 W. Which kettle transfers more useful energy to the water?
options: They transfer exactly the same amount
You cannot tell without the water's mass
gold.hint: Useful energy = efficiency × power × time. Work both out and compare.

misconceptions.message: Kettle A: useful = 0.88 × 2000 × 180 = 316,800 J. Kettle B: useful = 0.95 × 1800 × 180 = 307,800 J. Even though B is more efficient, A transfers more useful energy because its power rating is higher.

gold.display: Which statement about efficiency is correct?
options: A more powerful device is always more efficient
Efficiency can be greater than 100% if the device is very good
Wasted energy is eventually transferred to the surroundings, increasing the temperature
Renewable energy sources always have higher efficiency than fossil fuels

misconceptions.message: Efficiency can never exceed 100% (conservation of energy). Power and efficiency are different things. Wasted energy always ends up heating the surroundings, this is correct.

gold.hint: Think about conservation of energy and where wasted energy goes.

bronze.display: A heater receives 2000 J of electrical energy and converts 1600 J to heat for the room. Calculate the efficiency of the heater.

misconceptions.message: Divide useful by total, not total by useful. Efficiency = 1600 ÷ 2000 = 0.8.
Useful output (1600 J) is the heat for the room. Efficiency = 1600/2000 = 0.8.

bronze.hint: Divide the useful heat by the total electrical energy.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency compares the useful energy out with the total energy in: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.pre: Useful output (the heat for the room), in J =
guided_steps.hint: The energy that does the job you want is the 1600 J of heat.
Everything that goes in: the 2000 J of electrical energy.
This should give back the useful output.
guided_steps.done: Matches the 1600 J we started with, so 0.8 is right.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 0.8 (or 80%). Efficiency has no unit.

bronze.display: A motor has an input energy of 500 J and a useful output of 350 J. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = 350/500 = 0.7. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%.

bronze.hint: Divide useful by total, then multiply by 100 for a percentage.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency is useful ÷ total, then turned into a percentage: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.hint: The energy you actually get out: 350 J.

guided_steps.pre: Turn the decimal into a percentage: 0.7 × 100 =
guided_steps.done: That is the step people forget.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 70%.

bronze.display: An LED bulb has an input power of 10 W and a useful light output of 7 W. Calculate the efficiency.

misconceptions.message: You can use power values directly. Efficiency = useful power ÷ total power = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.

bronze.hint: You can divide powers directly: useful power over total power.

guided_steps.say: You can put power straight into the efficiency equation: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\) works with watts too.

guided_steps.hint: The light you actually get: 7 W.

guided_steps.done: Back to 7 W, so 0.7 is right.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 0.7 (or 70%).

bronze.display: A car engine receives 40,000 J of chemical energy from fuel and converts 12,000 J to kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 12,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.3 = 30%. Don't divide 40,000 by 12,000.

bronze.hint: Divide the 12,000 J of KE by the 40,000 J input, then times 100.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency is useful ÷ total, then as a percentage: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.pre: Useful output (the kinetic energy), in J =
guided_steps.hint: The energy you want: 12,000 J of KE.
The chemical energy from fuel: 40,000 J.

guided_steps.done: 30% of the fuel energy becomes movement.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 30%.

bronze.display: A kettle is 90% efficient. It receives 200,000 J of electrical energy. Calculate the useful heat energy transferred to the water.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.9 × 200,000 = 180,000 J. Convert 90% to 0.9 first.

bronze.hint: Turn 90% into 0.9, then multiply by the total input.

guided_steps.say: Here we know the efficiency and the total input, and want the useful output. Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input.

guided_steps.hint: Should return the 0.9 we were given.
guided_steps.done: Back to 90%, so the useful energy is right.

guided_steps.say: So the useful heat transferred is 180,000 J.

bronze.display: A power station has an efficiency of 0.35. The total input power is 800 MW. Calculate the useful electrical power output in MW.

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.35 × 800 = 280 MW.
Both values are already in MW, so the answer stays in MW. No conversion needed.

bronze.hint: Multiply the total input power by the efficiency.

guided_steps.say: We want the useful power out, knowing the efficiency and total power in. Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input.

guided_steps.done: Both values were in MW, so the answer stays in MW.

guided_steps.say: So the useful electrical power output is 280 MW.

bronze.display: A Sankey diagram shows a light bulb receiving 80 J of electrical energy. The useful light output arrow has a width of 8 J. Calculate the wasted energy.

misconceptions.message: Wasted energy = total input − useful output = 80 − 8 = 72 J. Energy is conserved.

guided_steps.say: Energy is conserved: total in = useful out + wasted. So wasted = total input − useful output.

guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.
guided_steps.done: Adds back to the 80 J input, so 72 J is right.

guided_steps.say: So the wasted energy is 72 J.

bronze.display: Which of these devices is the most efficient?
options: Device A: 500 J in, 200 J useful out
Device B: 400 J in, 300 J useful out
Device C: 1000 J in, 600 J useful out
Device D: 200 J in, 50 J useful out

misconceptions.message: Calculate each: A = 200/500 = 0.40, B = 300/400 = 0.75, C = 600/1000 = 0.60, D = 50/200 = 0.25. Device B is the most efficient at 75%.

bronze.hint: Work out useful ÷ total for each device, then compare.

silver.display: A motor receives 5000 J of electrical energy. It wastes 1500 J as heat and 500 J as sound. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Useful = total − all wasted = 5000 − 1500 − 500 = 3000 J. Efficiency = 3000/5000 = 0.6 = 60%.
Remember to subtract ALL the wasted energies (heat and sound) from the input.

silver.hint: Take BOTH wasted amounts off the input first, then divide.

guided_steps.say: First find the useful energy. Useful = total input − all the wasted energy.

guided_steps.pre: Add up ALL the wasted energy: 1500 + 500 =

guided_steps.hint: Take the wasted energy off the input.

guided_steps.say: Now apply \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.done: Both wasted amounts were removed first, so 60% is right.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 60%.

silver.display: A wind turbine has an efficiency of 0.40. In one hour it generates 720 kJ of useful electrical energy. Calculate the total energy input from the wind in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ.
Don't multiply: total input = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ. The total must be MORE than the useful output.

silver.hint: Divide the useful output by the efficiency to get the bigger total.

guided_steps.say: We know the useful output and efficiency, and want the total input. Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.hint: Useful divided by efficiency gives the bigger total.

guided_steps.done: The total (1800 kJ) is larger than the useful output, as it must be.

guided_steps.say: So the total energy input from the wind is 1800 kJ.

silver.display: A gas boiler is 92% efficient and provides 46,000 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy wasted by the boiler.

misconceptions.message: First find total input: 46,000 ÷ 0.92 = 50,000 J. Then wasted = total − useful = 50,000 − 46,000 = 4000 J.

silver.hint: Find the total input first (useful ÷ efficiency), then subtract the useful.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the total input, then the wasted energy. First rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.
Now the finish. Wasted = total − useful.

guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.
guided_steps.done: Adds back to the 50,000 J input, so 4000 J wasted is right.

guided_steps.say: So the energy wasted is 4000 J.

silver.display: A hydroelectric power station converts the GPE of falling water into electricity. 8000 kg of water falls through 50 m every second. The station has an efficiency of 0.85. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE per second = mgh = 8000 × 9.8 × 50 = 3,920,000 W. Useful output = efficiency × input power = 0.85 × 3,920,000 = 3,332,000 W.
Since the water falls every second, mgh gives energy per second, which is power in watts.

silver.hint: mgh each second is the input power; multiply it by the efficiency.

guided_steps.say: The falling water's GPE becomes electricity. Find the GPE gained each second, \(E_p = mgh\); because it is per second, that is the input power in watts.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply by the height to get GPE per second.

guided_steps.say: That is the total input power. Useful output = efficiency × input power.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.85, so the useful power is right.

guided_steps.say: So the useful power output is 3,332,000 W (about 3.3 MW).

silver.display: An electric drill has a power rating of 750 W and an efficiency of 0.60. Calculate the power wasted as heat and sound.

misconceptions.message: Useful = efficiency × total = 0.60 × 750 = 450 W. Wasted = 750 − 450 = 300 W.
Find useful power first (efficiency × input), then subtract from total to get wasted power.

silver.hint: Find useful power (efficiency × total), then subtract from the total.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the useful power, then the wasted power. Useful = efficiency × total input.
Now the finish. Wasted = total − useful.

guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.
guided_steps.done: Adds back to 750 W, so 300 W wasted is right.

guided_steps.say: So the power wasted as heat and sound is 300 W.

silver.display: A Sankey diagram for a coal power station shows 1000 MJ input. The useful electricity arrow is 350 MJ and the cooling tower waste arrow is 500 MJ. Calculate the energy lost through other waste pathways.

misconceptions.message: Total in = all out. Other waste = 1000 − 350 − 500 = 150 MJ. Energy is always conserved.

silver.hint: All the outputs must add up to the input; subtract the ones you know.

guided_steps.say: Energy is conserved: everything in must come out somewhere. Other waste = total − useful − known waste.

guided_steps.hint: What is left must be the other waste.
All the outputs should add to the input.
guided_steps.done: Adds back to 1000 MJ, so 150 MJ is right.

guided_steps.say: So the energy lost through other pathways is 150 MJ.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One efficiency equation, values already in the right form: divide useful by total, or multiply back to find a missing piece.
problem_bank.silver_description: An extra move first: subtract the wasted energy, rearrange for the input, or work out the energy before you divide.
problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two equations: find the useful energy (KE, GPE, or power × time) first, then bring in efficiency.

opener.title: How much actually gets through?
opener.display: An old light bulb is like a leaky bucket. You pour in 100 joules of electrical energy, but only 10 joules come out as light. The other 90 joules leak away as heat you can feel on the glass.

steps.pre: Out of every 100 J you put in, how many joules come out as useful light?
steps.hint: It is given in the story: the light output is 10 J.

steps.pre: So the useful fraction is 10 out of 100. As a decimal, 10 ÷ 100 =

steps.say: That number, 0.1, is the bulb's efficiency: useful out ÷ total in. Every question in this lesson is that one idea, \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\), sometimes turned around to find a missing piece.

bronze.display: A torch takes in 60 J of energy and gives out 45 J as light. Find its efficiency.

steps.say: Efficiency is useful ÷ total: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

steps.hint: The energy you want out: 45 J.

steps.done: Gone. Useful over total, that is the whole method.

silver.display: A fan heater takes in 3000 J. It wastes 600 J as sound and light, and the rest becomes useful heat. Find its efficiency as a percentage.

steps.say: Silver adds a step: work out the useful energy before you divide.

steps.hint: Take the wasted energy off the input.

steps.done: The extra move was just finding the useful energy first.

gold.display: A winch motor is 0.60 efficient. It lifts a 50 kg load to a height of 12 m. Find the total electrical energy it uses. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.say: Gold chains two equations. First the useful output, the GPE: \(E_p = mgh\).

steps.hint: Multiply by the height to get the GPE.

steps.say: Now rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

steps.done: Back to 5880 J, so the input is right.

steps.say: So the total electrical energy input is 9800 J.

bronze.title: Bronze: one efficiency equation
steps: Put the useful energy (or power) on top, the total underneath, and divide.
For a percentage, multiply the decimal by 100. Efficiency is always below 1 (100%).

example.question: A lamp takes in 50 J and gives out 20 J of light. Find its efficiency.

silver.title: Silver: one move before you divide
steps: Sometimes find the useful energy first: useful = total − wasted.
Sometimes rearrange: total input = useful ÷ efficiency, or useful = efficiency × total.
Then finish the division (or subtraction) and give a unit or percentage.

example.question: A motor takes in 800 J and wastes 200 J. Find its efficiency.

gold.title: Gold: chain two equations
steps: First find the useful energy: KE (\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)), GPE (\(mgh\)), or power × time.
Then use efficiency to reach the missing quantity, rearranging to total = useful ÷ efficiency where needed.
Convert units first (minutes to seconds), and keep energy with energy, power with power.

example.question: A hoist is 0.50 efficient and lifts 20 kg to 5 m. Find the energy input. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
